speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head U of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister share the significance of COP27 for Singapore, the Singapore delegation's contributions to the conference and expectations for COP28 to be held in the United Arab Emirates later this year?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Rising sea levels pose an existential threat to an island nation like ours.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must do our utmost to contribute to global efforts to combat climate change.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, we have very limited natural resources to generate green energy and rely heavily on traditional energy sources to keep the lights on and even to produce NEWater.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How can we balance the needs of our economy to protect livelihoods and to mitigate climate change and the rising sea level threat?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What factors did the Government take into consideration when it raised our climate targets to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These are ambitious goals, considering that we are a high-density city state and international hub operating one of the busiest seaports and airports in the world.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our value-added manufacturing, particularly in the chemicals, electronics and precision engineering sectors, our financial services sector, the information and communications industries are all energy intensive.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hence, I would like to ask how confident is the Government of achieving our climate targets while maintaining economic growth?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How will we manage the green transition and enforce compliance?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What are the Government's key strategies and policies that will help Singapore peak emissions earlier and reach net-zero emissions by 2050?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am concerned about the impact on our small and medium enterprises.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Would the Government provide an update on the measures to reach out to our SMEs and guide them in their journey to transform their operations and reduce carbon emissions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also commend our revised 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution, which was submitted after a public consultation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also thank the many activists and individuals on the ground who have worked tirelessly over many years for Singapore to be more ambitious on our climate goals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my speech last year, I shared the stories of Esther from CDL, Lastrina, Cheryl and Swati from SYCA, Xiang Tian from LepakinSG and Wei-Shan from YP.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They hold us accountable to our promises to future generations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Net-zero emissions by 2050 is an important but not an easy goal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government share how it intends for the public sector to achieve net-zero emissions by 2045 and for the nation to reach the goal of net zero by 2050?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Achieving net zero by 2050 has to be a whole-of-nation effort involving the Government, civil society, businesses and individuals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While we encourage individuals to adopt low-carbon practices, efforts directed at the industrial and energy sectors will have the most impact on our nation's carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, transitioning to a green industry will create more jobs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government share how it will move away from emissions-intensive industries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Government provide a roadmap for the nation in achieving net-zero emissions by ensuring that all 23 industry transformation maps are reviewed with the goal of net zero by 2050?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, our Singapore Green Plan 2030 was launched in 2021.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There is no lack of publicity about our efforts to achieve net-zero emissions and we have invested in various infrastructure projects such as electric vehicle (EV) charging points, the use of EVs, promoting green buildings and offering grants for energy efficient technologies, among others.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: These were commendable efforts and we have thus far kept up with the momentum, although it was eclipsed shortly by the outbreak of COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Today, we have learned how because of high energy prices, some countries have taken a step back to using coal to supplement their use of fossil fuels.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But there are also countries that stepped up their effort in moving forward to use clean energy and invested heavily in wind, solar and others.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, nearly half of the world's low-carbon spending took place in China last year, according to one research.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Every one of us has a part to play in our Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What Government support is there to help in this transition?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: From the individual's perspective, how will the Government ensure there are good jobs and good growth opportunities for Singaporeans amidst this Green transition from a little red dot to a little green dot?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, certain jobs and businesses will become obsolete.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Traditional enterprises that fail will affect livelihoods and invested capital and funds.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I speak as Chairman of our Inter-Ministerial Committee on Climate Change (IMCCC).

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The IMCCC works very closely with the various ministries, and the ministries, in turn, work very closely with the sectors that they are responsible for, and in particular, we work very closely with Minister Grace Fu and the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE).

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Today I will give a broad overview and each of the Ministries will elaborate, in detail, on the plans that they have specifically.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Inter-governmental Panel on Climate Change's Sixth Assessment Report warns that after 2030, it will become increasingly difficult to limit global warming to 2°C and we will face heightened and more complex climate risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At COP26 in Glasgow, countries pledged to act.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But recent conditions have made it more difficult to stay the course.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Russia's invasion of Ukraine, exactly a year ago, disrupted energy and food supplies, causing energy and food prices to increase in many countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Despite these external challenges, Singapore decisively stepped up our efforts against climate change last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In Budget 2022, we announced Singapore's intention to raise our climate ambition.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked about the considerations for raising our ambition – after all, we also are affected by external events and Singapore, as a small, alternative energy disadvantaged city-state, faces natural limitations on our climate action measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Chairman, first, climate change is an existential threat for us here in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As a low-lying island, we are vulnerable to rising sea levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Being densely built-up, we are prone to trapping heat in our urban environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Climate change poses risks to our biodiversity, food and water security, and public health.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: To mitigate climate change effects on Singapore, we must engage other countries to reduce their emissions worldwide.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We must do our best and do our part, so that we can shape international norms to bring us closer to our collective goals.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This puts us in good stead to capture new economic opportunities in the climate transition.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Poh Li San, Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Mr Louis Ng asked how we will meet our climate targets.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Government, through IMCCC, strikes a balance between ambition and practicality of action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Green Plan sets out how the Government, businesses and the community can work together towards a greener future.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This year, we will enhance our public procurement strategy and start making regular progress reports on public sector sustainability initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) and MSE will provide further details to this House.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will also continue to forge international collaborations on climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Prof Koh Lian Pin asked about the significance of COP27 and COP28.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At both COP26 and COP27, Minister Grace Fu co-facilitated negotiations on Article 6.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Article 6 rulebook enables cross-border cooperation through carbon markets, for countries to jointly fulfil their national climate targets, making it more efficient and easier for countries to reduce their climate emissions and on a global level.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The inaugural Singapore Pavilion at COP27 showcased our homegrown companies, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), youths and academics, including Prof Koh, to the international community.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For instance, Sembcorp Industries launched its carbon management platform, GoNetZero.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And one of GoNetZero's partnerships, with OCBC Bank, encourages clean energy adoption and decarbonisation, starting with Singaporean companies and scaling up to the region.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Overall, COP27 advanced workstreams to support the implementation of the Paris Agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Chairman, government action is necessary but not sufficient to achieve a low-carbon future.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Businesses need to act as well, and we will partner them in their sustainability journeys.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The industry sector contributes over 60% of our overall carbon emissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, to reach net zero by 2050, we must decarbonise at every level – the economy, each sector and individual firms – so that our businesses are ready to thrive in the green economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: All of us must now factor in the cost of emitting carbon.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And now that the carbon tax levels are known, companies can also plan with greater predictability.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This will make greener modes of production, investment and living more desirable.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The carbon tax collected will continue to support businesses and households.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will invest in green technologies and infrastructure, extend energy efficiency grants to businesses, and cushion our lower- and middle-income households from the impact of the carbon tax on electricity prices with U-Save rebates.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Government will enable the energy transition by securing greener sources of energy.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our National Hydrogen Strategy lays out the roadmap for the use of hydrogen which, with technological advancements, could potentially supply up to half of our power needs by 2050.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In the meantime, we continue to see how we can import green electrons.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about support for industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As a financial hub, Singapore has a head start in green financing services.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our industry sectoral roadmaps consolidate common challenges, allowing scale-up of promising initiatives and guide companies in positioning themselves to capture opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Ministry of Transport (MOT) and Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) will update this House on the sustainability plans for the transport and tourism sectors respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Small companies can drive sustainability efforts across their supply chains.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: One example is DTC World, a local SME specialising in corporate gifts.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It champions sustainable procurement and promotes sustainable consumption and it has received multiple corporate sustainability awards.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Many Singaporeans are passionate about sustainability – not many more than Mr Louis Ng.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will support you in challenging your passion towards making an impact.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For Singaporeans who may not yet have internalised climate change, understanding the implications of climate change on the environment and our society is the first step.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: MTI will describe how we will do so with industry players and training partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, global climate action is urgent.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: All countries, including Singapore, must honour our shared responsibility for our planet earth.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The IMCCC takes a whole-of-nation view to make sure our efforts are comprehensive and coordinated.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Businesses, communities and individuals have a key part to play.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The climate transition will be challenging, but it will be a rewarding journey, with opportunities for us to innovate and reimagine a greener and more sustainable future.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, let us work together, towards a better and greener Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is an opportunity for Singaporeans to take part in a national conversation on the values, priorities and policies we want to see going into the future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Implicit in a discussion on social compact though, is the notion of a society, but what does that society look like?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is the size and make-up of the population, what are the population dynamics and what are the impacts on our social and economic development?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government would, no doubt, have received a lot of views on population issues over the course of the Forward SG exercise: views on immigration policy, ageing population, encouraging marriage and parenthood, for example.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How has this informed the refinement of our population strategies?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And how do our population strategies support the refresh of our social compact.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means that soon, the number of citizens in the working ages could decline, a phenomenon that some other Asian countries, like Japan and China, are already facing.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we know and have been confronting the rapidly ageing population with low birth rate problem for some time now in Singapore, does the Government perform similar modelling and long-term projections, to understand what are the degrees of changes we need in productivity improvement of our resident workforce and immigration policies, to reach what target GDP growth for the next five to 10 years?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given that we have a much smaller population compared to Japan, if our Government has similar modelling and long-term projection exercises, do we involve our people in the process of formulating the models, and discussing the scenario options and opportunities?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we do not have such co-creation process yet, can the Government consider developing one with the opportunities for a significant number of Singaporeans outside the Government, including both young and old, to be part of the process?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The advantage of such an approach, guided by population projection experts and Government officers, is that more Singaporeans can have a deeper understanding on the issues and trade-offs, and own a stake in co-creating a future scenario that we aspire for our country and our future generations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government will consider my suggestion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some young parents have provided feedback to me that the Budget policies do help to ease cost of living and promote work-life balance for families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Government intend to better communicate the intent of these policy changes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition, how does the Government intend to encourage middle-income families with mothers in PME jobs to remain in the workforce after giving birth, as they have much to contribute to the economy?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The lapse of the FDW levy tax relief may also be interpreted as a signal that the Government is reducing support for working mothers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such tax reliefs make a significant difference to household finances, especially for families with more than one child.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Government can shed more perspectives about these policy changes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I appreciate the acknowledgement that monetary support alone has a limited impact in incentivising working mothers to have children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, a rounded approach is needed to create a conducive child-rearing environment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is where changes like increased Government-paid paternity leave come in.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What can we learn from other countries' best practices, to improve the Government's strategies to encourage Singaporeans to settle down and have children?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we encourage the wider society, such as employers and communities, to play a part in engendering a more family-friendly environment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the measures of success for this?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The decline in the TFR as a country becomes richer appears to be a fairly general phenomenon across countries, as people become richer, they choose to have fewer children, but make heavy investment in their children's education.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: If innovation requires creative and talented people and if the probability of being a creative and talented person is independently distributed among people, then it follows that a greater number of creative and talented people would be found within a larger population.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: If it is people who create ideas, then a decline in TFR means a shrinking workforce, which is likely to reduce the flow of innovative ideas.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Another point comes from recognising that, at any given moment in time, there coexists different generations of people within a given population.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is a certain number of young people who work and who have the capacity to pay taxes that fund items, such as health subsidies, that are predominantly received by a certain number of old and retired people.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A decline in the population size thus reduces the tax base supporting each old and retired person, making it desirable to increase population growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The question that can be asked is: what can be done to take advantage of work-from-home (WFH) arrangements to bolster family life and contribute to boosting the total fertility rate?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Arrangements, such as flexible work schedule and telework, are sometimes said to be ways to improve work-life balance.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, when workers schedule flexibility comes together with working long hours, this may lead to less job satisfaction and diminish ability to manage family life.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It appears that doing part-time work has tended to be the primary means for workers, especially women, to achieve work-life balance.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, employers across the whole economy might find it profitable to introduce some form of WFH arrangement in the workplace, even post COVID-19.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The organisation of work, as well as the promotion and compensation system, might be adjusted to enable workers who have a better control of their work schedule, while keeping their full-time employment status.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The organisation of the school system affects the behaviour of parents.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A perennial problem faced by parents is the amount of time that they feel they need to give to help their children with school homework.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Is it possible to introduce time in school after formal lessons, so that outside-the-school trained personnel can be hired with government subsidy to supervise these children with their homework?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Then, when the children return home from school, the parents can devote their time to bonding activities with them.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: With support from the Government, family day activities can also be organised during the weekends to further enrich family life.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To be able to work regularly on certain days in a week from home and being relieved to some extent from the need to supervise their children's homework, will allow parents to adjust their parenting style and possibly, their decision about having another child.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, an unexpected consequence of COVID-19 is that at a societal level, we found digital means to perform work-from-home at a reasonably productive level.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As husbands and wives find the employment landscape in the post COVID-19 world, potentially allowing them to spend more time at home, this could provide an opportunity to put in place policy measures to influence parenting styles and their decision on childbearing.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, you can take all your cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: She said, "Questions like these should not be forgotten.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Every now and then, we should revisit them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And even if we do not, Mr Louis Ng will make sure that we do".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Like many, I am happy we have doubled paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As Minister Indranee knows – and she bore the brunt of my repeated questions – I have fought for this for many years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We should remember that an IPS research found that our family policies continue to signal that childcare is a woman's responsibility and reinforce gender stereotypes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We should not do this overnight but can gradually increase paternity leave over many years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The times I spent with my children during my paternity leave were precious time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It is time we can never get back.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am glad we have doubled paternity leave, but we urgently need to look into increasing the usage of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As the Deputy Prime Minister said, "We want paternal involvement to be the norm in our society and we will stand behind all fathers who want to play a bigger role in raising our children." Indeed, we should but we know that only about half of fathers use their paternity leave and the key reason for this low uptake is the lack of workplace support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can we do more to help our employers, similar to how the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) supports employers when it comes to reservist obligations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Government work with companies more closely and consider more incentives to ensure their employees use both their paternity and maternity leaves?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Parents struggled during the pandemic to find time to look after their children who had COVID-19 or when their schools closed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Things are not getting any easier as we emerge from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For many, the lack of time to look after their children continues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Worse still, Hand Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD) is back which can keep children away from school for about two weeks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I experienced this first-hand when all my children got HFMD previously and COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Government knows many parents are begging for childcare sick leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Government knows how important this leave is and already gives it to public servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have been calling for childcare sick leave for many years because both our children and our parents need this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am sure Minister Indranee agrees as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And I agree too that we have to balance this with the needs of businesses, especially SMEs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: One of the best journeys has been my parenthood journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am grateful that I have three healthy, happy and crazy girls and I proudly share many stories of Ella, Katie and Poppy in this House.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But I have three children only with the help of IVF which is a physically and emotionally painful journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We can do more to help those undergoing IVF.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: IVF is extremely stressful for both husband and wife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: One doctor shared that some female patients were not allowed time off from work for their fertility appointments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: He has also shared he met some men who break down because they do not know how to accompany their wives without employer support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Some women may end up leaving the workforce because of this lack of workplace support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Government has urged employers to be sensitive to couples undergoing IVF.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But we need to do more than just urge.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This will support couples, send employers a clear signal, and trigger mindset shifts in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And finally, this pandemic has shown that working from home is possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Through many surveys, we know that people want this option.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Government has also shared many times how flexible work arrangements (FWAs) help businesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In his Budget speech, Deputy Prime Minister said that FWAs are a key component in helping parents manage work and family commitments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We cannot have a Singapore made for families without FWAs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I know we are implementing the tripartite guidelines next year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Businesses already had the experience of the past three years to structure themselves around FWAs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There is no better time than now to lean into FWAs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I should also say that I have spoken up so much about giving time because I have lost time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: My dad passed away just before his retirement, before he could spend time with his family after working so hard his whole life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I lost time with him that I will never get back.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I want to make sure no one goes through the pain I went through and still go through each day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Giving childcare sick leave, paternity leave, parent-care leave, fertility leave and all the other leaves I fought for is not just about the minutes and seconds, but about giving people precious time to spend with their loved ones while balancing work commitments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While our enhancement of the baby bonus scheme in Budget 2023 is welcomed, it is time we adequately address the root cause of the low fertility problem and tackle the concerns of parents and would-be parents alike.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More policies and spending should therefore be directed towards tackling deep societal, cultural and institutional issues that currently discourage women, with agreement from their male partners, from taking part in procreation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, address stereotypes of gender roles and establish the idea of equal shared responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we work on entrenching equal shared responsibilities, young mothers, who fear loss of time, identity, personhood and even employment, means they have more time to rest, pursue their aspirations and contribute to the community at large.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, men who try to take on greater responsibilities for caregiving will be able to put aside their fears of being discriminated against in the workplace or facing backlash for the lack of perceived work commitment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Earlier this year, I received an email from my company's HR to update employees about the parental leave enhancements from 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is regardless of the gender of the employee and there is also the option to take this flexibly over 12 months.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand that even Temasek has raised its paternity leave to about four months and maternity leave to about six months.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While not gender-neutral, nonetheless, it sets a workable example for the Government to follow when it comes to adequately giving prep time for parents to play their caregiving roles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, it takes a village to raise a child and we should go beyond merely adopting a practical approach to calibrating childcare leave provisions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, true flexible work arrangements only began commonplace due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: According to a June 2022 UOB study, almost half of Singaporeans have returned to the office full-time even though more than 80% prefer some form of flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I fear that that number is much higher today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A fellow Singaporean who is a new mother currently on maternity leave emailed me about some thoughts which resonate with me.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: She shared her how she was lacking the intellectual stimuli and adult social interaction that came with work.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Back to work too soon, he kept thinking about the time he was not spending with his daughter.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Let us push for longer gender-neutral parental leave at a policy level for the country and empower new parents with the choice to share parental responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The objective is to assist parents to lighten their financial commitment in raising children.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The CDA scheme consists of two components: First Step Grant and Government co-matching.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: CDA funds can be utilised at approved institutions for approved expenses, which includes basic educational fees, medical fees, purchases of vitamins and health supplements, optical appliances and payments for assistive technological devices.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I would like PMO to consider extending the use of CDA for purchasing milk formula and diapers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Parents are spending a substantial amount monthly on these two essential items.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In April and May 2017, many parents had voiced concerns on the price hikes for infant milk formula, asking for regulation of price and fair pricing.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These calls were also heard in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The cost of infant formula has not gone down since then.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I understand that the Government would like to encourage breastfeeding of newborns and infants, but many parents have to rely on infant formula for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Adding milk formula and diapers to the list of approved items would be much welcomed and bring relief to many parents, especially those from low-income households.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, two weeks ago, on 6 February 2023, Minister Indranee answered Parliamentary Questions on the decision not to prosecute the Keppel & Offshore Marine (KOM) executives involved in a corruption case.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She said that it was standard practice not to issue any statement if law enforcement agencies decided not to proceed after an investigation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if anyone has questions on the decision, the matter can be raised in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the answers given by her in Parliament were far from satisfactory.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely we would want to know in more detail why we have failed where others have succeeded.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want to know what were the facts uncovered during the investigation and which could not, which led to the decision not to prosecute.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister’s replies to several questions were however evasive, uncertain or “I don’t know”.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When asked by the Leader of the Opposition whether the Board of Keppel at the time when corrupt payments were made were aware, the Minister replied that she cannot answer for Keppel.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are not asking the Minister to answer for Keppel, we are asking for the result of CPIB’s investigation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whether or not constructive knowledge is an offence is beside the point.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Corruption is an offence and during their investigation of this offence, surely, CPIB would make it a point to find out which decision makers were aware of the act.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When asked about the witness who changed his tune, her answer was again uncertain: “I think the answer is yes” and “I do not have details of what exactly was said”.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When asked whether the six KOM executives involved were aware of and authorised the corrupt payments, she replied that she did not know because she did not conduct the investigations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whilst the Minister claimed that anyone with questions could raise them in Parliament, she did not come into Parliament equipped with sufficient facts or knowledge to answer those questions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This does not help the public maintain trust and confidence in our enforcement agencies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our zero-tolerance policy on corruption is there for good reasons.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we stand by while corrupt companies win contracts and prosper, while more capable but uncorrupt companies lose out in the competition, what kind of world are we moving towards?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Minister consider appointing a committee to consult the public on what questions they want answered and to get the answers to those questions from the relevant agencies?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Transparency and accountability is the way to convince the public that the investigation was conducted professionally and competently, and the decision not to prosecute is a sound and impartial one.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Experience in some European countries has suggested that a more equal distribution of parental duties can help to improve the fertility rate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Higher baby bonus is always welcomed to keep pace with inflation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the Working Mother Child Relief continues to be a disappointment to stay-home mothers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Stay-home parents contribute to society as much as working parents.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Government consider introducing appreciation of the contributions of stay-home parents in the form of CPF top-ups?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Chairman, we often have seniors appealing for PRs or citizenship as the rest of their families already are.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Take for example, at last Monday's Meet-the-People's Session, Mdm Wong appealed for her mother’s PR as they have been residing in Singapore since 1984.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Her father, siblings and families are all Singaporeans except for her mother.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Will ICA consider more favourably on seniors' PR applications especially those who have been residing in Singapore for decades and with strong family ties here?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: As one of the fastest ageing countries in the world, how are we ensuring that we have enough youths and working adults to support the expanding cohorts of the elderly?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Do we have an optimal old age dependency ratio to target at?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Is the Government prepared to review policies to reduce the old age dependency ratio through boosting our birth rates, attract Permanent Residents or new citizens?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While our population is increasingly digitally savvy, we still have a generation of senior Singaporeans who struggle to keep up with the pace of digitalisation, despite everyone’s best efforts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some are fearful of being left out and left behind totally.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to give them enough assurance so that they do not reject digitalisation altogether.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I would like to ask if the Government will continue offering non‐digital options for seniors to fall back on?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The implementation of National Digital Identity (NDI) has been successful and very useful.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With a mobile phone and data connection, much can be done from wherever and whenever.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With utilities such as the NDI, not only is convenience of services and transactions enhanced, security is improved too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: MacPherson Care App, for example, used MyInfo to make registration of seniors and volunteers much easier and more seamless.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And it also enabled us to verify identities, making it safer for seniors who may be served by the on‐demand volunteers whom they could be unfamiliar with.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, this solves a key problem for us when we were designing the app.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can the Government share more about the efforts in investing in the next bound of digital infrastructure and utilities, so as to support our Smart Nation drive?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government holds a diverse and vast amount of data, but such data is not easily accessible, and understandably so, by non‐government entities – such as community organisations hoping to do better for the community and businesses pursuing quality innovations – and this is perhaps also so between Government agencies as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But how can we avail some or more of such data in a secured environment that allows experiments and product testing, without compromising data privacy and security?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could the Government share more about the data sandbox?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And given the emergence of technology such as blockchain and cryptography, might there be scope for more curated Government data to be accessed in a safe, controlled and anonymous manner?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Since June 2020, more than 130,000 seniors have gone through the Seniors Go Digital Programme.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Making digital and online services a way of life is not a one-off effort.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How is the Government ensuring that people who are less digital savvy are not left behind in our drive towards a Smart Nation?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, can we consider more resources to provide peer support to trainers?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: That is, for seniors to train one another in learning how to communicate and transact online.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Given their similar life experiences, they understand how best to keep each other safe from scams.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, has Government carried out any surveys among seniors on their most urgent needs, in relation to digital inclusion?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And what proportion of the elderly require such help?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And my one request is a very simple one, and it is to ensure we never have an only digital programme, at least not in the short term.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, digital services are now becoming essential in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Ease and confidence of using digital services does encourage the use and adoption, especially for the less digitally savvy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can Minister share the Government’s assessment of the digital services experience for Government services?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For less digitally savvy users, what is the level of adoption of essential digital services?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How are we leveraging technology to make the digital services experience more natural and human or intuitive?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What are the design considerations for Government digital services?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are clear benefits of reach, access and speed to making digital first our strategy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we advocate digital to improve the delivery of Government services, I hope that we do not move to being digital only.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is not just to ensure that physical access to services is available and that no one is left behind, but also to recognise that engagement with citizens is one that has many touchpoints and channels.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is important is how we integrate the experience of citizens and their access to services through the various touchpoints.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Digital is a channel for engagement and delivery of services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The focus is serving the needs of citizens and enabling the best delivery of services to meet the needs of citizens.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can Minister share the Government's plans to make it easier for people to use digital services and apps to improve their digital experience?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A common complaint when accessing Government services is not knowing which agency to go to or having to deal with different agencies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Digital can enable collaboration across agencies and integration of the user experience to deliver a more seamless experience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: An important element of the digital experience is availability of support or helpline when there are questions or when the service does not go as planned.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can Minister also share the structure of support for help for citizens when the service experience does not go as planned?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The world – commerce, communications and much of how we live our life – are now inextricably intertwined, bound together in the digital sphere.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Into this mix, the murky underbelly of the real world has replicated itself into the digital one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Cyberthreats are now part of the digital landscape.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From identity theft, scams, ransomware, malware to national security threats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore is an important node in this interconnected world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What is the Government doing to strengthen and protect our digital systems and how our citizens can also play our part in helping in that process?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, at the Smart Nation Summit week closing dialogue in 2019, Prime Minister Lee in his speech mentioned for us being a Smart Nation is not about flaunting glitzy technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But it is about applying technology to solve real world problems that would make a difference to people's lives and across the whole-of-society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the roles of the Smart Nation and Digital Government Group is to develop digital enablers and platforms to raise economic productivity and catalyse innovation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that there are many proofs of concepts and technologies already developed, how can SNDGG partner and engage businesses and the community so that the businesses and the community can tap on the opportunities brought about by these technologies as we collaboratively work towards the next bound of Singapore as a Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we use this ecosystem of partnership between SNDGG, businesses and the community as a comparative advantage in light of rising business costs and increasing competition in attracting investments around the world?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I first raised this 16 years ago during the Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I pointed out at that time that the majority of countries have already lowered their voting ages to 18.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In response, then Law Minister Prof S Jayakumar highlighted that Malaysia's voting age was also 21 and Japan's was 20.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, today, Singapore is becoming an outlier in keeping the voting age at 21 years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of course, we do not need to blindly follow the policies of other countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, we must question the rationale for Singapore's stand.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is so unique about our youths aged between 18 and 21 that they should not be entrusted with the vote?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The answer from the Government more recently can be summarised in three points.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, it is said that voting requires experience and maturity and only at 21 does a person come of age to make adult's decisions and engage in activities that involve significant personal responsibility.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, youths aged 18 to 21 are able to express their views through other platforms such as in Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth's Youth Action Plan.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To the first point about only coming of age at 21, we already require those under 21 to engage in some very serious undertakings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Boys are enlisted into National Service by 18 years, required to carry weapons and vow to defend Singapore with their lives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since our policies treat them as adults for these undertakings, how do we justify depriving these youth of a say at National Elections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the second point about voting involving the election of the President and the Government, is that not the whole point?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It seems that most other countries trust their youths to vote for their president and government, but this Government does not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As to the third point about being able to give feedback on the Government's youth action plans, I think we can all agree that giving feedback is not the same as having your vote counted at the National Elections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, this House changed its position on section 377A of the Penal Code and decided to repeal it, noting that half a generation has passed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government will be similarly open-minded about lowering the voting age as well.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Mr Chairman, strong institutions and good governance are key in ensuring continued political and economic progress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans quite rightly expect high standards of conduct from our elected and public officials.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Maintaining public trust is crucial for the effective functioning of our Parliamentary democracy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How then can we better manage and minimise potential or even perceived conflicts of interest for our elected officials and in the Civil Service to ensure the integrity of our public institutions?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A possible way of managing and deterring potential conflicts of interest is to shine a stronger light of scrutiny on activities that serve to advance various interest groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This system is not perfect, but it is a good start.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Of course, such mechanisms are not silver bullets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But if they are designed well, they can go some way to reduce real and perceived conflicts of interest.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In doing so, they bolster the public confidence in our Public Service, Legislature and Government by enhancing understanding, full transparency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, COVID-19 has taught us that technology can transform service delivery.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we can always do better and explore how technology can better serve residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One common feedback about Government e-services is that there are too many apps and systems in place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many services are also embedded within agencies’ websites, which makes them difficult to access.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To complete a transaction such as getting a housing loan, one has to go through inter-related steps involving several Government agencies, before we can arrive at the process completion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Surely, we can do more in terms of process mapping, to make the digital service journey more seamless to residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On a broader note, how can we also leverage on the benefits of new and emerging technology, such as generative AI, to turbo-charge Government services and processes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One population segment that can certainly benefit from using technology to access Government services are seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, they are hit by a double whammy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, many are still not as familiar with technology as the younger generations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, I know some of my Yio Chu Kang seniors have missed critical Government announcements as all these are sent electronically, as emails or through Government service apps.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some seniors either do not know how to access this online information or are too afraid to click on the relevant websites for fear of being scammed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One obvious response would be to push on with training and education, such as those offered by the SG Digital Office.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should also aim to go digital as much as possible, while keeping physical services and touch points available for seniors who are not digitally savvy, to access public services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we remain agile and resilient to uncertainties, while avoiding a tech divide?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore’s success in responding to and managing unexpected emergency situations such as COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the importance of having an adaptable Public Service.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It includes working with the people and private sectors to tackle issues and Singaporeans’ needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One key aspect of adaptability is the Public Service’s openness to innovation and to embrace technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Technology has been deployed in the direct interactions between the Public Service and the citizens it serves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Within the Public Service internally, technologies such as ChatGPT are being explored to further enhance efficiency – so that our delivery of public services maximises the value of every tax dollar spent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the proliferation of different tech solutions since the launch of Smart Nation in 2014, it is perhaps time for consolidation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over the course of the pandemic, the Public Service has responded well to the rapidly evolving situation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I want to place on record our thanks to all in the Public Service, including our union leaders in the public sector, for going the extra mile and for tirelessly seeing us through these three years of toil and trouble, and seeing us through the entire pandemic safe and secure to the admiration of many countries across the globe.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These new skillsets also enhance the employment and employability of our officers in the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is in part due to the conviction of KOM lawyer Mr Jeffrey Chow in US court for his role in the corruption.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Chow is given a one-year probation which he could serve in Singapore and $75,000 fine.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: That may not be a heavy punishment to some, but it is still a criminal conviction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Earlier this month, the hon Ms Indranee Rajah told this House that no prosecution was mounted due to the lack of sufficient evidence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How were such moneys allowed to be paid out?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And how did they pass through the senior management's and auditors' scrutiny?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will any recovery actions be taken against any employees?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Notwithstanding the alleged evidential difficulties, the stern warnings might have inadvertently sent an alarming message that a Singapore-linked company can be involved in a case of serious corruption, but individuals involved may not be dealt with proportionately.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is not good news for the credibility of Singapore Inc, not to mention a GLC which should be leading by example.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Not long ago, there was also the bankruptcy of the crypto currency exhange, FDX, due to massive fraud.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong informed this House that losses to Singapore's taxpayers' monies from Temasek investment in FDX were limited.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But the company's management and owners still allegedly engaged fraud worth several billions of US dollars.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A shadow of potentially serious financial discrepancies hangs over the Adnani Group.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I said that it is startling that the existence of bribery contracts and payments somehow seem to have escaped the notice of Keppel's senior management, board of directors, audit committees and even the external auditors for 14 years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Could this point to the weaknesses in our company and auditing regime?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Among other suggestions, I had asked for the Government to review and enhance company regulations and suggested that the Government should consider having inspections and subject companies, directors and audit committee members to penalties for any non-compliance, and that the Government should review and enhance the requirements for whistle-blowing policies in companies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Rather, I am concerned about the potential rise of a view following recent cases that corporate governance standards in Singapore including Government-linked entities may not be what they used to be – and this should not be the case.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Following the disappointing outcome on the investigation by CPIB, what steps would the Government take to improve the corporate governance of our companies?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Specifically, what are the lessons we learn from how KOM was able to carry out the bribery acts of such magnitude and for so long?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What are the measures that Government intend to take to prevent similar cases from happening again?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am referring to the brazen bribery acts as well as the difficulties in prosecuting individuals even though KOM itself admitted liability and paid massive fines to foreign governments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the Government will take steps to improve corporate governance for our companies and I also hope the Government will ensure that Government-linked companies take adequate due diligence before committing on investment on public monies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In retaliation, the police arrests a high-ranking officer from the agency on what is believed to be a trumped-up charge of corruption too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This scenario may seem fanciful in Singapore, but unfortunately there has been precedent for such kind of behaviour elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, there exists anti-corruption provisions dealing with public servants in the Penal Code 1871.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Investigations under these provisions come under purview of the Police.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When I asked in this House whether there is utility in maintaining the Penal Code provisions which have not been used in the recent past, the Minister for Home Affairs felt that there is as these provisions are more targeted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He however accepted that these provisions should be ported over to the PCA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should put to bed this potential jurisdictional issue as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had recently suggested that PCA provide for extraterritorial reach with respect to Singapore registered companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is clear is that this case involved foreign bribery.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, to find jurisdiction under the PCA currently, one of the ingredients of corruption must have happened in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because there is no extraterritorial reach of the PCA vis-à-vis Singapore companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: CPIB’s stated policy in this House is that it will investigate all cases whether they happened locally or overseas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Lastly, Sir, there have been steps taken in other jurisdictions to enlarge the ability —

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members for their questions and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There were two categories on population and fertility as well as on corruption.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will take the cuts on population and fertility first, and Ms Hazel Poa’s cut on corruption, I will address later when I respond to the cuts on corruption.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the Forward Singapore exercise, we have spoken to many Singaporeans who have shared their views and aspirations for the future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As we work towards building the future we aspire to, it is important to understand the key population trends affecting us and how we must work together as one people to address them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As Ms Ng Ling Ling mentioned, countries around the world are facing demographic challenges brought about by ageing populations and declining fertility rates.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: South Korea’s Total Fertility Rate (TFR), currently the world’s lowest, dropped to a new low of 0.78 last year.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: China’s population also shrank for the first time in more than six decades, and their annual number of births nearly halved compared to six years ago.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Births in Japan have plunged to a record low.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Even Norway and Finland, who were previously successful in improving their fertility rates, are finding it difficult to sustain these gains.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Like other advanced societies, Singapore’s TFR has been declining for many years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was partly due to the Tiger year in the lunar calendar, which is generally associated with lower births among the Chinese.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But beyond that, there are longer-term global societal trends at play, which apply to us too.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While the aspiration to marry and have children remains strong, more are postponing marriage and more are also postponing having children or having fewer children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the same time, we are living longer.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With an ageing population, we will find it increasingly challenging to sustain economic growth as the growth of our resident workforce slows.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Caregiving needs will intensify as family sizes shrink and more Singaporeans will face the dual pressures of raising young children while caring for their elderly parents – and in fact this is already happening.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are also becoming a more diverse society.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have always been multiracial, multi-religious and multicultural.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While the proportions of our main racial groups remain stable among our citizens, our social fabric continues to evolve.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is therefore even more important to that we recognise this diversity as a core part of our identity, appreciate different cultures and their practices more and make this multicultural aspect of living in Singapore and being Singaporean, a strength.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These trends show the complexities and challenges on the population front.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our population strategies are key to managing these challenges.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar asked how these strategies relate to the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Through these conversations, Singaporeans have shared their views on the kind of Singapore we want to be and how we can forge our future together.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our population strategies take into account these views and seek to achieve a stronger social compact by strengthening assurance for Singaporeans throughout their lives, growing opportunities for Singaporeans through a vibrant and resilient economy and strengthening solidarity for a more cohesive society; as well as planning ahead for a better home for ourselves and for generations to come.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, we will continue to strengthen assurance for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A key aspect of this is the support we give to help Singaporeans realise their marriage and parenthood aspirations, among other life goals.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked what we can learn from other countries’ best practices to encourage Singaporeans to settle down.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Key elements that have made a difference elsewhere include societal norms that embrace children and families and encourage shared parental responsibility as well as a family-friendly workplace culture.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We need a whole-of-society effort to foster such norms and to build a conducive environment that values and supports families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For individuals, this is often about finding a work-life rhythm that is suitable for our different life stages as we pursue our family, career and other life goals.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And for employers, it is also about valuing employees’ family and overall well-being that could at the same time result in stronger talent attraction, retention and higher productivity for the employer.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is also about everyone doing our part to strengthen the overall ecosystem of support so that we have a family-friendly environment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the part of the Government, as Deputy Prime Minister Wong announced in the Budget statement, we are providing more support for the early stages of family formulation in a few areas.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are doing more to enable young Singaporeans to achieve their housing aspirations.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have also increased the CPF Housing Grant for first-timers purchasing resale flats.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Minister Desmond Lee will share more on these plans at Ministry of National Development’s (MND) Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These enhancements apply to eligible Singaporean children born from 14 February 2023 onwards.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have also extended the Baby Support Grant for eligible Singaporean children born from 1 October 2022 to 13 February 2023.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This represents an increase of up to $6,000 per child up to before the age of seven.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I hope this provides more assurance to couples like newly-weds Mr Ng Jia Jing and Ms Chia Shi Min, who are planning to have a child next year.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They are looking forward to the enhanced Baby Bonus Scheme which will help with their child-raising costs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This targeted financial help is in addition to existing subsidies for preschool, education and healthcare for all Singaporean children, and regular top-ups in each child’s CDA, Edusave and Post-Secondary Education account, including the most recent top-ups announced at Budget this year.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will also increase support for parents in managing their work and family commitments.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is a big step towards normalising and enabling fathers to play a bigger role in raising our children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As mentioned by Deputy Prime Minister Wong, we intend to mandate the additional Government-Paid Paternity Leave in time to come.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Ng asked about efforts to increase the use of paternity leave and proposed equalising the amount of maternity and paternity leave.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Louis Chua also spoke about shared parental leave.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our focus for now is to encourage and enable fathers to use the paternity leave that is available to them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Even as the Government increases paternity leave and stands behind fathers in playing a more active role in child-raising, we need shifts in societal mindsets and norms to encourage and support fathers in taking up this leave.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
