text: Workplace culture, in particular, the attitudes and mindsets of supervisors and colleagues will make a big difference in helping fathers feel assured about using their leave.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The take-up rate for paternity leave has gone up over the years and I hope to see it continue to increase.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I encourage every employer to consider providing this additional paternity leave and I urge supervisors and colleagues to be supportive when fathers take time off from work to care for their children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will also double Unpaid Infant Care Leave for parents with children below two years old from 1 January 2024 onwards.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Each parent will be able to benefit from an additional six days of Unpaid Infant Care Leave per year in the child’s first two years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Taken together, eligible parents will be able to take up to 26 weeks of parental leave in their child’s first year.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if we can increase childcare leave provisions to cover needs such as caring for sick children or provide leave for couples to seek fertility treatments.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are aware that employees need time off from work for these and other personal needs and commitments.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Apart from leave, another important strategy we are focusing on is to increase the adoption of flexible work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These include but are not limited to Work-From-Home, which Prof Hoon Hian Teck spoke about.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: FWAs are a sustainable way of providing more flexibility for workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is critical not only for caregivers of children but also for caregivers of the elderly.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A company that has put in commendable effort to make FWAs work for their employees is CBM Private Limited.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A facilities management company with 1,900 employees, CBM Private Limited has been adopting staggered working hours and Work-From-Home arrangements since 2017.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: During the pandemic, they further tweaked the staggered working hours arrangement to give employees more flexibility in their start times to avoid peak hour congestion.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They recognised that staff like security guards have to be on site and leveraged technology like roving robots to reduce manhours.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: CBM also set up a floating team of covering officers to take over from staff who have urgent family or caregiving duties.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: CBM shared that with FWAs, their employees are more productive, more focused and happier at work as they are better able to adjust their work schedules to manage both work and personal commitments.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While there may be adjustments to work processes and costs of implementing FWAs in the short term, FWAs can increase productivity, lower absenteeism and turnover, and increase employee engagement in the long term if implemented well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Embracing FWAs as a workplace norm will help Singapore companies stay ahead of the competition and better attract and retain talent.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The tripartite partners have developed a set of best practices for employers to voluntarily adopt under the Tripartite Standard on FWAs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Ng asked if we can implement these Guidelines earlier as well as consider legislating them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Even as we encourage more FWAs, we need to make sure workplace harmony is maintained.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The best way to achieve this win-win outcome is not by taking a legalistic approach at the onset but to focus on shaping norms and fostering workplace trust.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Beyond these measures, there were other suggestions to improve support for parents and to better recognise their efforts in bringing up their children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have received feedback from parents about the difficulties they face in accessing reliable infant care arrangements when they return to work.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the Forward Singapore Care Pillar efforts, we will be reviewing how we can better support new parents in caring for their infants.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This should help in defraying expenditure in these areas.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Hazel Poa suggested recognising the contributions of stay-at-home parents through CPF top-ups.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Many of our marriage and parenthood measures are given regardless of the parents' employment status, including our recently enhanced Baby Bonus Cash Gift and Child Development Account.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I hope these enhancements and plans will give greater assurance to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, we want to grow opportunities for Singaporeans amidst a more uncertain global economic outlook.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Economic growth over the past few decades has generated good employment and business opportunities for Singaporeans as well as the resources to support public infrastructure, healthcare and education.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling spoke about the decline in the number of Singaporeans in the working ages and asked how we will achieve economic growth to generate more opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Indeed, with a slowing resident workforce growth and a maturing economy, we will have to work harder to restructure the economy to sustain economic growth.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Economic growth is driven by new ideas, new technologies and output from the work of people.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Even as we strengthen efforts to enhance our overall productivity, there will be a limit to economic growth if companies do not have enough workers with the necessary skills to support their businesses and activities here.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the Empower and Equip pillars of Forward Singapore, the Government is looking into ways to further develop our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This includes preparing our students well for jobs of the future by providing access to good quality education and diversifying pathways in schools.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We invest heavily in the upskilling of Singaporeans and help them to strengthen career health and reach their full potential.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also want to build a stronger pipeline of Singaporeans for leadership positions across different sectors of the economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Even as we strengthen the quality of our local workforce, there are not enough Singaporeans to meet all our economic and social needs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Remaining open to foreign manpower brings benefits to countries by filling skill shortages in the labour market, boosting the productive capacity of the economy and supporting innovation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some segments of the foreign workforce support the caregiving needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Other foreigners help companies in Singapore grow by filling manpower gaps.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Companies, including Singaporean-owned ones, have been raising concerns about the lack of sufficient local workers and the need for foreign manpower.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Global talent, such as those coming in on the Overseas Networks and Expertise (ONE) Pass or Tech.Pass, also bring in investments, new business operations, technology and job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These measures ensure that the foreign workforce complements rather than displaces the local workforce.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will also continue to transform our economy and industries to create better jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the Industry Transformation Maps, we are pressing on with economic restructuring, automation and redesigning jobs for higher productivity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government will continue to work with our unions to support industry and our workers as we transform our economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We must be prepared to work together as a society to smoothen the transition.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There will be new technologies and processes to adapt to.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some roles could be replaced with new ones and so we must all reskill and take on new functions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Also, with higher wages, a part of increased business costs may be passed to consumers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While these cost increases may be calibrated to manage the impact on overall cost of living, we must still be prepared to pay more in the longer term to fairly value the work and services provided by our fellow Singaporeans in jobs currently with lower wages.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will benefit in the long run with a more productive economy, better jobs and higher wages for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Next, I will talk about the need to strengthen solidarity and maintain a cohesive society in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I had earlier spoken about how one in three citizen marriages is transnational.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As Singaporeans venture overseas for school, work and travel, they may meet and marry non-Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some return to Singapore to start and raise a family here.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are also others who meet and marry foreigners based in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singapore is also an attractive place for skilled people who come here to work, given our connectedness, security and quality of life.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Over time, some of them may share our aspirations and ideals, and may want to make Singapore their home.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We should welcome those who are prepared to make the long-term commitment to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh spoke about reducing our old-age dependency ratio by boosting our birth rates as well as taking in new Permanent Residents and citizens to support our ageing population.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While our policies do not seek to achieve any optimal old-age dependency ratio, welcoming such immigrants continues to play an important role in moderating the impact of ageing and low birth rates in our population.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Most of our Permanent Residents and New Citizens granted each year are aged 40 and below.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have seen how tensions over immigration in other countries have led to fissures and divisions in society.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We must not let that happen here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While most Singaporeans understand why we need immigrants, there are, understandably, concerns over competition for jobs and other resources and how the texture and character of our society could change and whether our infrastructure can keep up.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked about trends in the number of new citizenships and Permanent Residencies granted.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At last year's Committee of Supply, I explained how COVID-19-related travel restrictions and safe management measures had slowed down in-person processes for the grant of citizenship or PR.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A number of approved applicants in 2020 and 2021 had yet to complete the in-person processes and some applicants who had intended to apply during that period were also unable to complete their own processes to submit their applications.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Hence, some of these applications were rolled over into 2022.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We consider very carefully who we take in as immigrants.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This ensures that new immigrants are rooted, able to integrate and contribute meaningfully here.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: All new adult citizens come from within our pool of Permanent Residents.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This means they have been in Singapore for some time already.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second-generation Permanent Residents serve National Service and in the process, forge bonds with other locals and contribute to the nation's defence.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: During the Forward Singapore engagements, Singaporeans reiterated the importance of safeguarding our identity as a multicultural and diverse society.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To do so, we must remain open to people of different backgrounds and cultures.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We must welcome newcomers and help them integrate into our society.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the same time, newcomers should respect our values and norms and make an effort to adapt to our way of life.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government has been working with our partners to develop resources and conduct activities to help foreigners settle in and understand our local norms and culture.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is a whole-of-society effort where different stakeholders including newcomers, Singaporeans, community groups and businesses all have a role to play.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To illustrate this better, let me share the story about the friendship between Margaret and Heidi.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Margaret Hou became a Permanent Resident last year.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She has lived in Singapore for the last 10 years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She regularly volunteers at community events and interacts with residents from different social and ethnic backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She takes the effort to interact and forge friendships with locals.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Her ex-colleague turned friend, Ms Heidi Yeo, who is Singaporean, appreciates Ms Margaret's willingness to help whenever they had to work closely together in their respective job areas.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They continue to meet up and help each other even though they are no longer colleagues and their friendship has blossomed over the years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Heidi shares Singapore culture and history with Margaret, which helps Margaret to gain a deeper understanding and appreciation of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Margaret in turn pays it forward by helping other newcomers to integrate into the local community through chat groups, monthly meet-ups and monthly sports or family activities involving local Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such friendships show us how both locals and newcomers can make efforts to foster integration and how we can come together to strengthen our bonds with each other and our sense of belonging to Singapore despite being from different backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is what the Unite pillar of the Forward Singapore exercise is all about.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We continue to plan for the long term and steward our scarce resources for both present and future generations.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling asked whether the Government has long-term projections to understand how we should adjust our population policies to achieve desired outcomes for Singapore in the future and how Singaporeans can be involved in the process.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have engaged Singaporeans in thinking about our future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, as part of the Long-Term Plan review, we engaged Singaporeans of different age groups and backgrounds extensively to better understand how our land and infrastructure plans can meet their aspirations and future needs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Through the Build and Steward Pillars of Forward Singapore, we will further explore how we as a society can build a greener, more liveable and more sustainable home for all.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Planning for the future is a complex process.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will have to consider what our future population will look like, not just in terms of size but also composition and make-up.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And this is contingent on many factors – various demographic trends, such as birth rates, life expectancies, and migration, as well as future social and economic needs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For instance, we need manpower to build our homes or care for our seniors, but the numbers could change with evolving family structures and the health of our ageing population.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our businesses’ manpower needs may vary, depending on the types of industries in our economy and ongoing economic transformation efforts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As our workforce continues to evolve in tandem with economic transformation, their needs too will change.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our aim is, as it always has been, to build better lives for current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our population policies are all aimed at this objective.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Looking beyond 2030, it is critical that we will continue to plan ahead of time, to maintain the flexibility to adjust our plans, respond to new trends and safeguard options for the future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will help us to provide a good quality living environment and home for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, in conclusion, I have laid out our population strategies and the key considerations behind them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the coming years, our demographic realities will only become more keenly felt.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our ability to nurture a high-quality workforce while attracting the complementary foreign manpower we need, and to integrate newcomers into our society while maintaining social cohesion, will become ever more important for Singapore's future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is a delicate balance and much will depend on how circumstances evolve.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But we will continue to work hard to build a Singapore with the well-being of Singaporeans at the heart of it, with opportunities for all, a society where families matter and are supported and where we can be united even in diversity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Everyone – individuals, families, communities, businesses and Government – has a role to play in ensuring that Singapore continues to be a home with opportunities, assurances and a strong sense of solidarity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Together, let us work towards a better future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the interest of time, let me jump straight to the lessons we have learnt since we started our Smart Nation journey in 2014.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first lesson is to always put people first.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most transactions can be completed from the comfort of their homes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singaporeans can use MyInfo to apply for credit cards, or LifeSG to access parenting, housing and other digital government services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Abundance is a restaurant bar that started out as a home-based business.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When it first opened in 2021, it used the GoBusiness portal to apply for the necessary licences.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This helped it to be set up quickly without having to go from agency to agency physically.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This progress motivates us to further improve, and as Ms Jessica Tan suggested, leverage digital technologies to improve our service delivery.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, the team at Open Government Products built the Health Appointment System last year to make it easier to book pneumococcal and flu vaccination appointments.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It has facilitated more than 40,000 appointments to date.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This system will soon be expanded for eligible women to book a subsidised HPV2 vaccination appointment.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will make it easier for our women to protect themselves through vaccinations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By April, the system will also allow appointment bookings for all vaccines under the National Adult Immunisation Schedule, and by June, vaccines under the National Childhood Immunisation Schedule.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To use digital tools with confidence, our citizens must be able to trust that they are safe.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With ever-evolving cybersecurity threats, this has become a tall order.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Alex Yam asked about protecting our digital systems.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are investing efforts to build stronger defences to safeguard people from scams and online harms.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will be launching a ScamShield Chatbot later this year on WhatsApp, to allow the public to report scam messages to the relevant authorities more easily.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA will say more about their efforts to address scams.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are also improving government ICT infrastructure to be more resilient against cyber attacks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are working with agencies to modernise and secure their key systems.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes moving more government systems to cloud, to improve resiliency, security monitoring, and our threat detection tools.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Mr Alex Yam pointed out, the Government cannot do all of this securing alone.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have launched the Vulnerability Rewards Programme to work with "white hats", or ethical hackers, experts and volunteers to identify weaknesses in our systems so we can continuously improve their security.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI)’s Committee of Supply debate, I will expand on efforts to uplift digital literacy and strengthen safety online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third lesson is that to go far, we must go together.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, we are collaborating with and learning from, leading countries and companies in Artificial Intelligence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We recently signed MOUs with Israel and Korea, as well as with Google and Samsung.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also have AI research partnerships with industry, such as with SembWaste to improve environmental sustainability through efficient recycling, such as using computer vision to sort waste.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to learn from the best-in-class, incubate good ideas and support Singapore companies in leveraging AI.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More importantly, we must never leave our citizens behind in our Smart Nation journey.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To points raised by Mr Seah Kian Peng and Ms Tin Pei Ling, we will continue our efforts to ensure our digital services are accessible and easy to use, for all.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also continue to provide non-digital options for critical government services for the foreseeable future.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In terms of design, which Ms Jessica Tan asked about, it is based primarily on following the user journey, identifying and fixing pain points in advance and rigorous testing.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing will speak more broadly about public service delivery, which Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will share more on our digital inclusion efforts during MCI’s Committee of Supply debate, particularly, to support the lower-income and seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, these lessons we have learnt are shaping the way we are thinking about the next bound of Smart Nation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During the various Forward Singapore conversations, it has become more evident how technology can enable and improve our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In MCI’s Digital Readiness Survey, 84% of Singaporeans agreed that digital technologies have made their lives easier.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As we refresh our Smart Nation strategy, three broad areas will be particularly important.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, enhancing opportunities for Singaporeans to flourish; second, ensuring trust and safety in the digital world; and third, strengthening our communities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, digital technology presents immense opportunities for Singaporeans and our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Ms Tin Pei Ling pointed out, it is critical to invest in digital infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked how we can better support our businesses and citizens to grow and thrive in an age of technological advances.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Q&M Group now plans to deploy this AI model to more than 150 clinics in the region.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: AI Singapore also runs the AI Apprenticeship programme to provide training using real world projects and help the trainees get better jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to nurture innovative use of data just as AI Singapore and Q&M Group have done, including taking in Ms Tin Pei Ling's suggestion for us to find more opportunities to securely share government data with businesses and the community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are already exploring the use of emerging privacy-enhancing technologies that allow us to share data in a seamless and secure manner, to nurture more collaboration with non-government entities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A second priority is to ensure that we can go digital with confidence, feel safe and secure using digital tools and services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have also developed PhishMonSG in collaboration with MHA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a tool that proactively hunts for phishing sites that pose as Government agency websites, so that we can remove them before they can harm the public.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also want to help level up our companies, especially small and medium enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third area of priority is to help strengthen our Singapore communities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our Smart Nation must be inclusive, so that all Singaporeans can participate fully in an increasingly digital society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As I have said, digital first need not mean digital only.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is also value to co-create with the community, promote opportunities for people and groups to come together to make Singapore a better home for all of us.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I encourage companies and research institutes to submit proposals to address these real-life issues, and possibly pilot them in the JLD soon.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, the task of building Smart Nation, like that of building Singapore – is never done.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to find ways to leverage technology to realise new opportunities for our people and businesses, to help our people go digital with confidence and to build a stronger community.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, I will now address the cuts from Mr Murali Pillai, Ms Hazel Poa and Mr Dennis Tan, pertaining to our anti-corruption efforts and on corporate governance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I wish to thank Mr Murali Pillai for his support for CPIB's work and continuing interest in improving our anti-corruption efforts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali gave an example where, due to the overlap in jurisdiction between the Police and CPIB, there could be a risk of senior officers taking retaliatory action against one another.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under our system of criminal justice, charging decisions are decided by the Public Prosecutor (PP), who makes these decisions independently.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Therefore, Mr Murali can rest assured that there is no room for Police or CPIB officers to raise trumped-up charges against one another, or against any one for that matter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali renewed his call for CPIB to consider extending the extra-territorial reach of the PCA, to companies incorporated in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Insofar as companies are concerned, the CPIB expects Singapore-incorporated companies operating overseas to operate in compliance with the laws of the countries that they have a presence in.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For corruption-related offences, one needs to establish the mens rea of the alleged offender, to show the requisite corrupt intent.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where the alleged offender is a company, the focus of investigations would generally be on the individuals who are the controlling minds or decision-makers of the company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For companies incorporated in Singapore, such individuals can be both Singaporean or non-Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, this applies even if they are officers of companies not incorporated here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The current extra-territorial reach of the PCA is therefore already quite broad and effective.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The practical impact of Mr Murali's proposal is that if a company is incorporated in Singapore but involved in corrupt activities conducted overseas by non-Singaporean individuals and there is little connection to Singapore other than the fact that the company is incorporated here, the CPIB will nonetheless be obligated to investigate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While Singapore is firmly committed towards international anti-corruption cooperation consistent with our legal framework and international commitments, it would be a stretch to empower or require the CPIB to investigate activities taking place entirely outside Singapore, involving non-Singaporean actors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have already seen the challenges in investigating activities by Singaporeans committed abroad.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Investigating the activities of non-Singaporeans abroad will be even more so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have to take a realistic view of the efficacy of doing so, given the evidential difficulties we can expect where material evidence and key witnesses reside outside of Singapore, and out of CPIB's reach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali also suggested a review to allow for a non-conviction-based confiscation mechanism to deal with assets believed to be acquired through proceeds from corruption.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where a person has been convicted of corruption, the PCA provides for the disgorgement of the gratification received.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, there are existing powers to confiscate outside of a conviction, which apply if qualifying circumstances are met.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Mr Murali noted, the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 allows for confiscation without conviction, but only where the accused person is deceased or has absconded.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Further, under the Organised Crime Act 2015, it is possible to obtain a non-conviction-based confiscation order to disgorge ill-gotten gains from a person involved in organised crime activity, which includes corruption-related activities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government is committed to disgorging any financial benefit derived from offenders' predicate offences, which include corruption.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But in the same vein, we need to ensure that the power is fairly scoped, particularly where the Court has not arrived at a determination of guilt.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And she also asked whether we could consider appointing a committee to consult the public on what questions they want answered and to get the answers to those questions from the relevant agencies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think the Member may not be familiar with how such matters are dealt with.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They do not, as a general rule, provide details of investigations, for good reasons, including to avoid prejudicing any action that may have to be taken subsequently if new material facts come to light, or adversely affecting informants or witnesses who may then become less willing to offer assistance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As explained before, where there is public interest in knowing more details, Members may file questions in this House and the relevant Minister will, after consulting the PP, answer the questions to the extent permitted by law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is the role of Members of Parliament (MPs) to raise relevant and appropriate questions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do not set up committees to find out questions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As to answering of questions involving investigations, the Minister answers to the extent permissible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Minister is not involved in the investigations or charging decision and therefore would not have personal knowledge of the details.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Poa raised several assertions as to the answers that I gave in Parliament earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She said that answers had either not been given or were evasive and raised a couple of examples.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will deal with those examples in a minute.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But first, I would like to remind the House that there were 16 Parliamentary Questions and I answered all of them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The questions that came up subsequently were supplementary questions of which I had not been given any prior notice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And of those, I had to deal with the questions as and when they were put to me in the Chamber.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first of these was raised by Ms Poa.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She referred to the Leader of the Opposition's question as to whether investigations included determining the constructive knowledge of the Keppel board at that time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I sought clarification from him and he had confirmed he was not suggesting that this was an offence under the PCA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, I think Ms Poa raised the question of mutual legal assistance (MLA).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She said that, when asked about MLA requests, I replied I did not know all the details of the MLA but that, for at least one or two of the latest ones, there were no response.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the Member wishes to quote me, I would be grateful if the Member quotes me accurately.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: AGC and CPIB also sent an MLA request to another relevant foreign authority to interview another potential material witness.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then, I said the contents and outcome of these MLA requests are confidential, but I can inform the House that they have either not yielded evidence that could be used to secure a conviction before our Courts, or the responses have not been helpful in advancing the case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, whatever the number of MLA requests, the outcome of these were that the information produced did not yield evidence that could be used to secure conviction, or they were not helpful in advancing the case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, I was asked a supplementary question about the MLA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I said that I did not know all the details, but I did know that, for the latest ones, there had been no response.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, Ms Poa said that when asked about the witness who changed his tune, my answer was allegedly uncertain.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She claimed I said, "I think the answer is yes" and "I do not have details of what exactly was said." That is a summary of something I said right at the end.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Poa did not inform this House of what I said at the beginning.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would be helpful if I do that, because again, it would be good if you are going to quote somebody, to quote them fully.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to that witness, I had said, "So, the question is, has he said something different here?" And I said, "I think the answer is yes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, I wish to put on record that the questions that were put to me were answered and answered fully to the extent that I was able to and within the ambit of the law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Her suggestion is whether we could appoint a committee to consult the public on what questions they want answered and to get the answers to those questions from the relevant agencies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I would like the Chamber and all Singaporeans to understand what this request actually means.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What it means is that we set up a committee, open to the public and we ask everybody "what questions do you want to ask".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then, because she is not saying, "Come back to the Chamber to ask the question", she is saying "Let us ask these of the agencies".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, this is something which every investigating office in the Police and other investigation agencies should take note of because it would mean that your entire investigation file will be open for questions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is also something that every AGC officer should take notice of, because your entire file will also be open to question.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is also something that every witness who has given or will be giving evidence in response to a request to assist the Police or any investigation agency: everything that you say, everything that you would have told them, even before it is brought, to Court, even before it is proven, could well go out to a committee who will be asking you, "What about this?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What about that?" And all of these before it is proven in Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the ambit of the question that has been asked.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the answer is that it is not appropriate to do something like that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The proper process is that MPs, knowing what the ground or the public wish to know, come to Parliament, raise this in due process and the Minister will answer to the best of his or her ability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I turn now to the questions and comments raised by Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Essentially, his broader thrust was about corporate governance in general.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But he did make a point where he said that the public found it difficult to understand how, in the Keppel case, CPIB could not find a single person that they could charge.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is not something which is lacking on the part of CPIB, but it is the nature of cross-border international corruption cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, I take the point about the need for good corporate governance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They were required to put in place a whole slew of improved corporate governance measures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They have also, I believe, the entire Keppel Group, taken on board the global best practice to mitigate bribery risks in an organisation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think that is referred to as the ISO37001: Anti-Bribery Management Systems.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In respect to the broader corporate landscape, listed companies are required under Singapore Exchange (SGX) listing rules and principles under the code of corporate governance, to put in place sound internal controls and risk management frameworks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are expected to institute and disclose whistleblowing and anti-corruption policies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Boards are also expected to establish the appropriate culture, values and ethical standards of conduct at all levels that support the prevention, detection and reporting of wrongdoing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I should also mention that there is a spectrum of complementary legal and regulatory provisions in place to ensure that companies, directors and their officers have good corporate governance practices and do not engage in corruption.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, listed companies are subject to the listing rule requirements and principles under the code of corporate governance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Those require them to have internal controls and risk management frameworks, as I mentioned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, companies act through their directors and key executive personnel, who owe fiduciary duties to the company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Directors are required under the Companies Act to discharge their duties honestly and with reasonable due diligence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A director who takes a completely lackadaisical attitude towards the company's affairs or actively encourages its officers to engage in criminal activities could face criminal liability for acting in breach of his or her duties owed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Of course, there are other statutes that apply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CPIB has also been proactively engaging companies to strengthen their controls against corruption.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Besides sharing best practices, companies in the ACPN are encouraged to undergo the ISO 37001: Anti-Bribery Management Systems certification, which I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ultimately, businesses have the responsibility to keep their own houses clean and to comply with the prevailing laws and regulations of jurisdictions where they operate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: By adopting a strong anti-corruption culture and actively reporting corrupt behaviour, companies in Singapore will reinforce our anti-corruption efforts and advance the reputation of Singapore as a trusted business and investment hub.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The findings from the recent CPIB's 2022 Public Perception Survey affirms our national anti-corruption strategy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ninety-six percent of the respondents surveyed rated Singapore's corruption control efforts to be effective – an increase from 90% in 2016.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, incorruptibility is a key part of the Singapore DNA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This did not happen by chance but is the hardearned result of our strong political will, effective anti-corruption laws, the society's unwavering support for zero-tolerance towards corruption and an effective CPIB that is committed to investigate any allegation of corruption, without fear or favour.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chairman, on behalf of the Prime Minister, let me first address the cut by Ms Sylvia Lim on voting age.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Some of them regretted doing so when the political outcomes were not as they had expected, although they would not say so publicly for political reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Others were not clear if this had led to better governance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The opinions of our youths are indeed important.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The majority of our youths under the age of 21 are in our post-secondary institutions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We do regularly and proactively engage our youths on national issues and societal issues to take into account their views in our decision-making and policy formulation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth, National Youth Council, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Social and Family Development and other Government agencies do this on a regular basis.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: An example is the Conversations on Singapore Women's Development in 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The views surfaced in these dialogues were considered in the White Paper, which was tabled in Parliament last year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, if we take a step back, the evergreen challenges for any democracy is how do we deliver good governance and a good government.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The key to that lies in two things.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, how do we have good people with the right values and right capabilities to stand forth to serve?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, how do we encourage every voter to not just think of his or her individual interests, for the here and now; but also for the wider interests of our society and future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, there are policies and guidelines that help organisations and individuals to avoid and manage situations of potential conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Officers who engage in external activities and may have potential conflicts of interest have to do the necessary declarations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For Members of Parliament from the People's Action Party (PAP), our Prime Minister issues the Rules of Prudence after every general election to remind ourselves of the standards that we should hold ourselves to.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I cannot say this for other Members of the House, but I think what is set out by the Prime Minister for PAP Members of Parliament should be applicable to everyone in the House, because as Ms He said, we are all elected officials and we all owe a duty to our society to maintain the high standards that we expect of ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, while these policies and guidelines are in place, it is equally important to have people with good character and judgement to make decisions on specific cases or situations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Third, where lapses occur, there must be processes in place to make things right and subsequently update and strengthen our system to prevent recurrence.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This three-pronged approach must be refreshed and updated regularly so that we can maintain our hard-won reputation as a society that is corruption-free and with high integrity amongst our public officers and elected personnel.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, I will address the cuts by Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This month, we stepped down from DORSCON Yellow to Green for the fight against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I would say that the fight is not over yet.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Public Service will lock in the lessons learnt from COVID-19 and apply them in our ongoing Public Sector Transformation efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have reinforced four key lessons for good governance in an uncertain world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, harness the strengths of the people and private sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, COVID-19 reinforced the importance of officers from different agencies working together to address citizens' issues in a citizen-centric way.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to organise more services around citizens instead of along agency lines.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To Mr Saktiandi's point, technology is indeed a key tool in achieving this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As part of the Digital Government Blueprint, we have achieved almost 100% digital service delivery.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to integrate and redesign services and processes in a manner that is meaningful and intuitive to citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: An example is the recently launched "Care Services Recommender" digital service which provides personalised recommendations on areas such as care services and financial support schemes to caregivers based on their needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This helps caregivers to find the right services and schemes across agencies quickly, easily and from one place.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While digitalisation has helped to improve services for most Singaporeans, we acknowledge Mr Yip Hon Weng's point that some citizens, including elderly citizens, may still need physical transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Hence, we are also building a network of physical ServiceSG centres that aim to be a one-stop concierge for citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Today, we have two ServiceSG Centres at Our Tampines Hub and One Punggol and four smaller satellite centre nodes at Community Clubs (CCs), each offering hundreds of services from over 20 agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Officers at these centres can advise citizens on the suite of services that can help them, based on their circumstances and needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: ServiceSG is opening one more satellite centre at Bukit Canberra CC by the middle of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This will make integrated Government services even more accessible to more citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The second lesson from COVID-19 is the value of partnership with the people and private sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Take, for example, how the various sectors rallied together to secure essential supplies for Singaporeans, distribute masks and hand sanitisers and reach out to affected families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our future challenges will be more complex, requiring whole-of-nation efforts to overcome.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Public Service must build up the mindsets and the skillsets to work with the private and people sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: During the past few years, we have set up structures such as SG Healthcare Corps and Alliances for Action (AfAs) to aid us in saving lives and livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is also why we want to send more officers to outside the Public Service to gain exposure and build new networks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The third lesson from COVID-19 is that our organisations and people must be agile.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: During the pandemic, the Public Service has managed to stand up large inter-agency operations and deploy manpower nimbly at short notice.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They took on roles such as safe distancing ambassadors, officers handling dormitory operations and call centre agents managing public's queries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Without formal structures in place, we had to rely on agencies to redeploy manpower at short notice or individual officers to volunteer to cover the manpower gaps.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I am heartened that our agencies and officers have actively leaned in, across agency boundaries to support our battle against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many officers have also gained new competencies and forged new connections along the way.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The fourth lesson from COVID-19 is the importance of building forward planning capabilities while managing current operations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It developed a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test during COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There will be other crises in our future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Public Service must retain our muscle memory in crisis management and strengthen our forward planning capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To Mr Patrick Tay’s point, we are upskilling our officers to meet new demands in a post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This requires our officers to acquire skills in areas such as scenario planning, risk identification, data analytics and sense-making.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These skills are not only useful in crisis, but also in the Public Service’s work in a dynamic and uncertain world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To achieve this, we continue to actively invest in training our officers to build broader and deeper competencies in their respective domains.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is further reinforced with a range of “learning by doing” development opportunities such as structured job rotations, inter-agency gig work and bite-sized attachments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chairman, I would like to conclude this segment by thanking all our public officers for their contributions over the past three years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our public officers have not only worked hard, but also applied innovation and worked across agency lines to achieve a common mission – to safeguard lives and livelihoods. "One Public Service" is not a slogan.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is something that we live by, it is something that we believe in, and it is something that we want our officers to have in their DNA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: COVID-19 served as a glue to bring all sectors – public, private and people – together for a larger and higher purpose.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As we work together to build Singapore towards SG100, I hope that this partnership will be continuously strengthened, so that we can all better serve Singaporeans and Singapore together.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In my speech, I made reference to the respective jurisdictions of the Police and the CPIB in investigating corruption offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I was really referring to investigative powers such as invoking the power of arrest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I do appreciate the hon Minister's point about the charging decision, which is, of course, reserved to the public prosecutor.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Nonetheless, I appreciate the hon Minister's response, that the CPIB does not need a porting over of the provisions in the Penal Code and I may have to address this matter with the hon Minister for Home Affairs as to whether these provisions in these circumstances would be obsolete and should be repealed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I think we know that fathers in more labour intensive jobs are taking less paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Could I ask that at least the Prime Minister's Office could deep dive into this and look into specific jobs with the lowest paternity leave usage and see how we can focus our efforts on helping employees in those jobs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Second on fertility leave, could the Prime Minister's Office at least look into launching a pilot whereby we can give fertility leave to public servants first and see whether that has been effective in helping some of our public servants for a start?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, with respect to paternity leave, indeed it is a whole-of-society effort and we want to encourage employers and employees in all occupations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the areas that Mr Louis Ng has identified would certainly include areas where we want to encourage more take-up of paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to his second cut which was for public servants, we always look into the suggestions of Mr Louis Ng with all due seriousness and we will do so in this case.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I just have one clarification for Minister Indranee.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: The 6.9 million population target was first set out in the 2013 Population White Paper.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I wanted to ask, will the Government consider doing a milestone progress review involving young people?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I appreciate that population projection is a very complex matter, but will we at least involve tertiary students or young professionals who are trained in statistics, in economic modelling, in sociology?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Because they were too young when the White Paper was set out in 2013, but they will be the group that will be in the prime of their working years when we reach 2030, when one in four are above 65 and they will have to shoulder quite a high burden.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: So, I just wanted a clarification on that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Sorry, could I just clarify with the Member, because she was describing about the young people but I was not sure I heard the question at the end of it.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: The question is whether the Government or the National Population and Talent Division (NPTD) will consider doing a review of what was projected in the 2013 White Paper on population, which had the mention of the 6.9 million population target by 2030, especially young people who are in the tertiary level now and young professionals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I just feel like asking the Chamber, "Everybody, all together now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is a planning parameter." It has been mentioned so many times.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to the Member's suggestion, what we do is, at regular intervals, the Ministries look to see what needs to be done in planning terms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I think that what we will do is whenever appropriate, the relevant agencies and Ministries will put out the figures or the data that they think is necessary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In terms of engaging people, as to what should go into those plans, we will do that as well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: First of all, I just wish to say that whatever I have said that was said by Minister Indranee all came from Hansard.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I did not put words in your mouth.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But I do accept your point that these were supplementary questions and therefore, that could have contributed to the words that conveyed uncertainty and I should not have read too much into it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I do not believe I have heard the answer to that.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Can the Minister give us the reply to those two questions now or if it is not at your disposal, if we were to file Parliamentary Questions again, would we get answers to that?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Member may ask the question again, but I do not think the answer is going to be any different and let me explain why.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They do not, in the course of investigating an offence, go and look for things which are not offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, six individuals, insofar as offences under the PCA are concerned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because when an agency goes in, an agency has to investigate something which is under its remit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You do not go and investigate, let us say, theft, and then start asking whether somebody has committed adultery or whether somebody has committed some other form of offence, unless it has come to your attention.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And these six individuals, who they feel are implicated; they cannot clear the evidentiary burden.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, they clearly feel that something is not quite right, but they just cannot clear the evidentiary hurdle.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What that tells us is that CPIB has done as much as it can within the remit of the law and that remains the position.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, even if the Member were to ask the question again, the answer will not differ.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Can I just then get confirmation that CPIB did not look into whether the board of directors were aware when they were investigating?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Because you said that they did their investigation and narrowed down to the six individuals.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But when they started the investigation, they would probably be looking at a wider range of individuals who may be involved.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, does that not include whether or not the board of directors were involved?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: And did they find out whether the board, or did they ask or try to find out whether or not the board is aware?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: And with regard to the six KOM executives, you said that you are unable to answer whether they authorised the payment because you are not privy to the investigation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Can I ask whether it is not permitted by law for you to answer the question about whether or not they authorised the payment?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As to the second question, I have answered it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will be the third time I am answering it, and the answer is the same.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I was asked that question, I believe, by Mr Louis Chua, if I am not mistaken.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And my answer was, I do not know.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They do not disclose this to the Executive.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And this is a very odd thing because for all that some political parties talk about independence and separation of the Executive, they keep trying to get into what ought to be an independent activity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The CPIB has made its investigations, they have arrived at the conclusion that six individuals are implicated and that is as far as I can go.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not know the answer to that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For this particular answer, it is not that I am not permitted in law to tell you.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if you ask, should I go and ask CPIB this, the answer is, it is not appropriate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I should not be interfering in a CPIB investigation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Executive should not interfere with an investigation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that is something which is very important for Members in this House to understand.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Let the agencies do their work independently, and we should not be going and interfering with their investigations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What was the first one she reiterated, I am sorry?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Whether when CPIB did the investigation, did they also investigate whether the others were involved?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Yes, so, again, my answer has not changed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When CPIB goes in, they look for commission of an offence and people who may have committed an offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if something is not an offence, then obviously they would not be pursuing that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is as much as I can say.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Chairman, clarification for Minister Chan Chun Sing on the issue of voting age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In other countries, we have seen that where there is military conscription, there can be a link with the age of conscription to the voting age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, for example, in the US, we saw that in the 1960s, there was a big move to bring the voting age from 21 to 18 because teenagers were being conscripted to fight in the Vietnam War.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The slogan at that time was "Old enough to fight, old enough to vote".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I would like the Minister to explain to our youths, why they are old enough to fight and defend Singapore with their lives, but they are not old enough to vote.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Chairman, I think the answer to Ms Sylvia Lim's question had been given previously, but if I may just remind the House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we look at the rights and responsibilities of all our people, from the age of 16 until 21, there is a gradation of scale.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At different ages, they have different rights and different responsibilities; and Ms Lim might want to refer to our previous answer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: On the KOM case, so far, we have always been talking about the criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But such a big case for our country, there is also a lot of implication on corporate governance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I would like to ask a question on corporate governance: for these six individuals – and maybe there are even other individuals – these things have happened and it is a very big case.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And KOM is a Government-linked company or a Temasek-linked company, so I think that it is within the interest of Parliament to be able to understand the case better.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have, specifically, this interest: are the six individuals, after the case had happened, were they still under the employment of the company?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Did the company relieve them of their responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second question, now that they have gotten the warning letter from CPIB, did the company, retrospectively, go and impose some penalties on the six individuals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For example, as far as I know, some companies can take back their bonuses, the bonuses that they have learned in the past, based on these cases that they have now found out that these businesses that they have done in Brazil is not proper, but they could have gotten bonuses and other monetary benefits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, is KOM as a company, going to do that?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because this has a lot of implications on corporate governance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Whatever we say about zero tolerance and all that, if all these things are not done, then whatever we say in this Parliament is not going to be credible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not have it with me today, but there is a paragraph in there, which says that Keppel investigated at the material time when this thing came up.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I had better check, but for some, there were penalties or sanctions, in terms of whether their bonuses — okay, I do not want to be inaccurate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And those were complied with, because when the DPA expired, the charges were withdrawn, which means that KOM did comply.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Prof Koh Lian Pin, would you like to withdraw the amendment?

text: Chairman, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
